claims.statement: The control plane receives its entire deployment configuration through the typed `Env` interface in `packages/control-plane/src/types.ts` — D1 `DB`, the `SESSION` Durable Object namespace, `REPOS_CACHE` KV, `MEDIA_BUCKET` R2, optional queue bindings (`IMAGE_BUILD_FINALIZATION_QUEUE`, `AUTOFIX_QUEUE`/`AUTOFIX_DLQ`) and service bindings (`SLACK_BOT`, `LINEAR_BOT`), secrets, and plain-text variables — assembled in production by Terraform (`workers-control-plane.tf`), which binds provider vars conditionally on the selected backend and enabled bots.

`env-validation.ts` enforces the full encryption-key contract, not mere presence: a key must be present, strictly base64 (whitespace rejected), and decode to exactly 32 bytes for AES-256, because a short key would silently downgrade to AES-128/192 and a malformed one would otherwise only fail at the first secret write mid-spawn; failures carry the generation hint `openssl rand -base64 32`.

Secrets-at-rest encryption is not optional at runtime: the SessionDO graph construction (`createSessionRuntime`) calls `requireRepoSecretsEncryptionKey` and `requireTokenEncryptionKey` before building components, so a missing or malformed key fails every session request at initialization instead of persisting plaintext; secrets routes and MCP server stores likewise refuse to operate when `REPO_SECRETS_ENCRYPTION_KEY` is absent.

Credential encryption is split into three independent key domains — `TOKEN_ENCRYPTION_KEY` for SCM enrichment tokens in `user_scm_tokens`, `REPO_SECRETS_ENCRYPTION_KEY` for repo/environment/global secrets, MCP credentials, and the commit-signing private key, and `PROVIDER_ACCOUNTS_ENCRYPTION_KEY` for subscription-provider account credentials (Terraform generates and persists a dedicated 32-byte key when the operator does not supply one).

`SANDBOX_PROVIDER` selects the sandbox backend (`modal` default, `daytona`, `vercel`, `opencomputer`, `e2b`); `resolveSandboxBackendName` defaults an unset value to `modal` and throws on anything else, and `createSandboxProviderFromEnv` throws with explicit per-backend messages on missing credentials while parsing numeric/boolean settings (e.g. `E2B_AUTO_PAUSE`, `DAYTONA_AUTO_STOP_INTERVAL_MINUTES`, `VERCEL_SNAPSHOT_EXPIRATION_MS`) at construction so invalid values fail immediately.

Sandbox provider construction happens during SessionDO graph assembly, deliberately: both `resolveSandboxBackendName(env.SANDBOX_PROVIDER)` and `createSandboxProviderFromEnv` run in `createLifecycleManager`, so a misconfigured backend fails every session request at initialization rather than surfacing at the first spawn.

Terraform enforces the per-backend env contract at plan time with `variables.tf` validation blocks (e.g. `modal_token_id`/`modal_token_secret`/`modal_workspace` required when sandbox_provider = 'modal', `daytona_api_url`/`daytona_api_key`/`daytona_base_snapshot` for daytona, and the e2b/vercel/opencomputer equivalents), and `locals.tf` binds only the selected backend's variables to the worker.

Image-build capability is a separate, centralized policy: `image-builds/provider-policy.ts` permits `modal`, `vercel`, `opencomputer`, and `e2b` and rejects Daytona with the message "Image builds are only available when SANDBOX_PROVIDER=modal, vercel, opencomputer, or e2b"; the web app mirrors the same list in `packages/web/src/lib/sandbox-provider.ts` so UI copy cannot drift.

`SCM_PROVIDER` selects the single source-control provider per deployment: `resolveScmProviderFromEnv` trims/lowercases, returns the `github` default when unset or empty, accepts only `github`/`gitlab`/`bitbucket`, and throws a permanent `SourceControlProviderError` otherwise; the router caches the resolution keyed by the raw env value and `enforceImplementedScmProvider` answers 501 when a route's `supportedScmProviders` excludes the deployment's provider (the bitbucket case) and 500 when the configuration itself is invalid.

On GitLab deployments `GITLAB_ACCESS_TOKEN` is required for API access and is threaded into the sandbox provider config for git auth, while `GITLAB_NAMESPACE` scopes repository listing to a group; `createSourceControlProviderFromEnv` only constructs the GitLab credential block when the token is present.

User-editable integration settings are persisted in D1 across three tables: `integration_settings` (global defaults keyed by `integration_id`), `integration_repo_settings` (per-repo overrides keyed by `(integration_id, repo)`), and `integration_environment_settings` (per-environment overrides, an owned child of `environments` with ON DELETE CASCADE), created by migrations 0007 and 0038.

`IntegrationSettingsStore` validates every settings write against the runtime Zod schemas in `packages/shared/src/types/integrations.ts` (the source of truth for all persisted settings types) and re-parses and re-validates stored JSON on every read, so corrupt rows surface as `IntegrationSettingsValidationError`; repo keys and `enabledRepos` entries are lowercased on write.

`getResolvedConfig` resolves settings through a generic later-layer-wins merge — global defaults, then repo overrides, then environment overrides (design §13.5) — in which undefined keys never clobber, and the `enabledRepos` allowlist comes only from the global layer where undefined normalizes to null (all repos), `[]` is the disabled state, and a non-empty list is a case-insensitive allowlist evaluated against the repo (never against the environment).

Only the session-scoped integrations `sandbox`, `code-server`, and `vnc` (`ENVIRONMENT_SETTINGS_INTEGRATION_IDS`) accept environment-level overrides: `supportsEnvironmentSettings` gates the store methods, and the environment-settings routes reject other integrations with 400 and verify the environment exists (404) before reading or writing.

The GitHub `autofix` object is the one exception to the flat resolution merge: repo-level autofix fields deep-merge into the global autofix policy instead of replacing it, so a repo can set `maxAttemptsPerPrPer24Hours` without clobbering the global `enabled`/`allowedReviewBots` settings.

Sandbox settings are re-normalized at control-plane boundaries via `normalizeSandboxSettings`: writes use `invalid: "throw"` (storage errors on invalid values), while stored global/repo/environment blobs and resolved configs are normalized with `invalid: "omit"` so stale rows drop invalid keys instead of poisoning spawns.

Session-scoped integration settings — code-server enablement, VNC enablement, and sandbox settings — resolve from the session's primary member (position 0 of the repository list, the scalar mirror) with the environment's overrides layered on top when the session launches from a saved environment; `enabledRepos` allowlists stay evaluated against the primary repo; a repo-less session falls back to global sandbox defaults with code-server/VNC disabled; and resolution failures degrade safely to disabled/empty defaults.

The primary-member scope rules are consumed uniformly: `handleCreateSession` and the automation scheduler's `launchChild` both call `resolveSessionScopedSettings` with the member list and environment id, child-session spawn inherits the parent's primary repo plus environment for sandbox settings, and MCP servers are the deliberate contrast case, resolving as a union across all session members in `McpServerStore.getDecryptedForSession`.

The Slack agent-notify gate applies the same primary-repo rule on a different call path: the lifecycle manager resolves it live from the scalar mirror via `IntegrationSettingsStore.getResolvedConfig("slack", ...)`, and it short-circuits to disabled when `SLACK_BOT_TOKEN` is absent so a misconfigured deployment never installs a tool that would 503 on every call.

Model enablement is deployment-wide user configuration stored as a single global row in the `model_preferences` D1 table: `PUT /model-preferences` validates every id against `VALID_MODELS`, rejects an empty list (at least one model must stay enabled), and upserts the normalized `provider/model` ids; `GET` reconciles the stored list against the shared catalog — dropping unknown ids via `normalizeValidModels` and falling back to `DEFAULT_ENABLED_MODELS` when the list empties, no row exists, D1 is absent, or storage fails — logging a reconciliation event when repair was needed.

Model preferences are enforced at session creation: child-session spawn loads `getEffectiveEnabledModels` (stored list, else `DEFAULT_ENABLED_MODELS`) and rejects requests for disabled models with `Model "…" is not enabled` (400) or returns 503 when preferences are unavailable, while `resolveEnabledModel` applies the fallback policy of desired-if-enabled, else fallback, else first enabled.

SCM settings (`alwaysUseDraftMode`, `pullRequestLabel`) are a top-level, provider-agnostic setting kept deliberately outside the integration framework: `ScmSettingsStore` reuses the generic `IntegrationSettingsStore` and its two tables under the fixed storage key `scm` (no schema migration), the shape forbids `enabledRepos`, and the session runtime resolves global-defaults-merged-with-repo-override at PR time via `resolveScmSettings`, retaining built-in defaults when D1 is absent.

SCM settings are served SCM-agnostically on both GitHub and GitLab deployments (`SCM_AGNOSTIC_USER_OR_SERVICE_ROUTE`) at `/scm-settings` and `/scm-settings/repos/:owner/:name`; malformed settings are rejected with 400 before storage and storage failures map to 503 "SCM settings storage unavailable", pinned by `scm-settings.test.ts`.

Commit signing is deployment-wide configuration in the singleton `commit_signing_configuration` D1 row (`singleton_id = 1`): the OpenSSH Ed25519 private key is stored encrypted with `REPO_SECRETS_ENCRYPTION_KEY` and never sent to a sandbox, while the public key, `SHA256:` fingerprint, and committer identity are plaintext; `PUT /commit-signing` validates the strict request schema and derives the public key/fingerprint from the unencrypted `ssh-ed25519` private key, and a missing encryption key yields 503 "Commit signing encryption is not configured" rather than any plaintext path; all commit-signing responses set `Cache-Control: no-store`.

The sandbox signing bridge keeps the private key control-plane-side: `GET /sessions/:id/commit-signing` returns only the runtime configuration (committer identity plus public key) or an explicit `{ enabled: false }` on non-GitHub deployments, and `POST /sessions/:id/commit-signing` accepts a payload bounded to 1 MiB on both sides, verifies the `X-Open-Inspect-Signing-Fingerprint` header matches the configured key (409 on key rotation), signs with the decrypted key, and returns the armored SSHSIG signature; the in-sandbox git signer (`gpg.ssh.program` shim) posts the commit payload with the sandbox auth token and fingerprint header.

Secrets are user-editable key/value configuration encrypted at rest in D1 (`repo_secrets`, `global_secrets`, `environment_secrets`) with three scopes served by `routes/secrets.ts` and `routes/environment-secrets.ts` (global, per-repo, per-environment, plus value-free import); list endpoints return metadata only — never values — and every handler refuses with 500/503 when `REPO_SECRETS_ENCRYPTION_KEY` or the DB is absent.

Secret key/value validation is shared across scopes: keys must match `[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*` (max 256 chars, uppercased), values max 16 384 bytes, at most 50 secrets per scope, and a reserved-key list (`PYTHONUNBUFFERED`, `SANDBOX_ID`, `CONTROL_PLANE_URL`, `SANDBOX_AUTH_TOKEN`, `PATH`, …) prevents a secret from clobbering the sandbox boot environment; validation failures map to 400.

Merged secret payloads are capped at 128 KiB (`MAX_COMBINED_SECRETS_BYTES`) with per-source byte attribution, and `SECRETS_CAP_ENFORCEMENT` controls the outcome: the default and any unset/garbled value is fail-closed `enforce` (spawn/build rejected with `SecretsCapExceededError`); only the literal `warn` logs and proceeds.

The web app's `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` variables (`NEXT_PUBLIC_WS_URL`, `NEXT_PUBLIC_SANDBOX_PROVIDER`, `NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_NAME`, `NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_ICON_URL`, `NEXT_PUBLIC_SCM_PROVIDER`) are inlined into the client bundle at build time, so Terraform sets them as build environment (OpenNext/Cloudflare) or Vercel project environment variables and also writes them into the generated `wrangler.production.toml`; changing one requires a web rebuild rather than a redeploy.

The web app's `SERVICE_AUTH_SECRET` is its per-service sig1 signing secret and must equal the control plane's `SERVICE_AUTH_SECRET_WEB` binding, which Terraform generates as a 64-character `random_password` in state (operators read the generated value rather than inventing one); `dispatchWebServiceRequest` throws "SERVICE_AUTH_SECRET not configured" when absent and signs every outbound request as `service: web` after stripping caller-supplied `Authorization`/actor/service-signature headers.

The Modal data plane receives its configuration as Modal secrets created via CLI or Terraform — `llm-api-keys` (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`), `github-app` (`GITHUB_APP_ID`, PKCS#8 `GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY`, `GITHUB_APP_INSTALLATION_ID`), and `internal-api` (`MODAL_API_SECRET`, which must match the control plane's binding, plus the SSRF allowlist `ALLOWED_CONTROL_PLANE_HOSTS` restricting which hosts sandboxes may call back into).

Deployment admission is configuration-gated twice: four comma-separated allowlists (`ALLOWED_USERS`, `ALLOWED_EMAILS`, `ALLOWED_EMAIL_DOMAINS`, `ALLOWED_GITHUB_ORGS`) admit on any match with `UNSAFE_ALLOW_ALL_USERS` as the explicit bypass, and Terraform's `checks.tf` hard-fails the plan when no allowlist is configured and the unsafe flag is unset, also requiring a complete OAuth pair for at least one sign-in provider with a compatible admission rule.

Sandbox lifecycle env configuration: `SANDBOX_INACTIVITY_TIMEOUT_MS` (default 600000 = 10 minutes) feeds the lifecycle manager's inactivity config, `EXECUTION_TIMEOUT_MS` (default 5400000 = 90 minutes) backs both the session watchdog (overridden by a session's persisted `sandboxTimeoutMs`) and the automation recovery sweep, and `LOG_LEVEL` (default `info`) is parsed per entrypoint.
